children: Venture investors have poured billions into startups aiming to capitalize on White House priorities.
One fund says this is the wrong approach.
Commonweal Ventures has raised $54 million in new capital to expand its strategy of backing startups that work with the government regardless of which political party is in power.

"We are trying to underwrite political risk. If we believe it'll go out with the political winds we avoid it," said Nate Loewentheil, founder and managing partner of Commonweal and a former economic-policy adviser in the Obama White House.

Loewentheil said he believes many venture firms today back startups that serve signature Trump administration issues, such as the Golden Dome antimissile shield, putting such investments at risk should Democrats take power.
Commonweal is staying away from such key-agenda items, Loewentheil said. Similarly, the firm avoided electric-vehicle startups during the Biden era.
"So there are two traps in government-driven markets: signature policies, which get reversed, and rhetoric, which produces hype cycles disproportionate to any real shift in spending," he said.

Commonweal raised a $51 million Fund II and a $3 million co-investment fund from the State of New York. It plans to back about 20 pre-seed and seed-stage startups in sectors including healthcare, government services, energy and public safety.
The firm does invest in startups that sell to the Pentagon or work in clean energy, as long as they aren't dependent on marquee government programs.

Each portfolio company partners with the public sector in areas with broad support from governments, which serve as customers, investors, research and development partners, regulators or market makers.

"There's no doubt that a needle has to be threaded," said Michael Catanzaro, an adviser at Commonweal and a former White House senior energy adviser during President Trump's first term. "There are very few issues that the Hill agrees on," he said, referring to Congress.

Commonweal has built out an advisory board with officials who had served in the prior five presidential administrations, including Catanzaro and Carol Browner, former administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency in the Clinton administration.
Political overlap exists, Catanzaro said, such as around the threat of Chinese dominance, the need to invest in domestic critical minerals extraction, and the build-out of reliable power sources.

Commonweal has avoided the more divisive issues, Catanzaro said. "The high-profile, high-priority, campaign-promise policies that a president or presidential candidate will run on, those are the things that have such a big target on their back for a future Democratic administration to come in and roll back," Catanzaro said.

Commonweal's first fund was a $23.2 million pool. As of June 30, the fund generated about 17% in net internal rate of return, and a net total value to paid-in capital of 1.5 times, according to the firm. That puts the fund above three-quarters of venture funds from the same vintage year in terms of performance as of the first quarter of this year, according to the latest information available from Carta, a software company that tracks private markets data.

Commonweal's first fund backed 21 startups, including Concourse, which modernizes legacy information systems; Crux, which provides a capital-markets platform for clean and critical infrastructure; Starbridge, which provides market intelligence for government contractors; and Advocate, a provider of software for easing interactions with federal benefit programs.
